Dr. Das is a very nice person and it's clear that she wants the best for her students. I also truly believe that she has a vast knowledge when it comes to Global Modernism. However, it is also clear that her teaching skills definitely fall short to make her qualified enough to transfer that onto us, which I'm sure she is also aware of. Firstly, she has difficulty connecting the general to the specifics. This manifests in two ways: in connecting the general theories on modernism to specific applications in modernist texts and also in connecting general ideas about a novel to its specific passages and techniques. Secondly, she seems to look at every text or theory from a global modernist/postcolonial perspective. I understand that it is usual for professors' area of specialty to influence their teaching and also that in the 21st century it is impossible to teach a modernism class without mentioning global modernism and postcolonialism. HOWEVER, how can one learn to read global modernism, without fully grasping the modernisms of Eliot, Pound and Woolf? This is not to say that we did not discuss those in class, but to say that every time we discussed their texts, our discussions (if you could call them discussions) could not pass the obvious facts that Pound was a fascist, Eliot was a monarchist and that Woolf was a pro-imperialist (exaggerated for comedy purposes but you get the point). Often times this course felt like a postcolonial class and I am not sure if I learned enough about British modernism, which I find necessary at least for an undergrad level. Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, her classes are not structured well enough. She seems to come to class with a general idea, and not specific points or passages to talk about and discuss. For a 170 page long novel, we spent three weeks discussing the first 40 pages. And I do not even know how those three weeks went, because almost no one was talking in class, since most had lost interest or had given up. Sad.
